stem: All four refiners agree in a group chat to fix pump prices and rotate winning bids for municipal fuel. The finance manager who typed the minutes claims the deal was oral and informal so no agreement exists. Is the cartel per se prohibited.
answer:
Yes. The cartel is per se prohibited in both limbs, the pump-price fixing and the rotation of winning municipal-fuel bids, and the finance manager's oral-and-informal defense fails to negate agreement.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 14(a), approved July 21, 2015, restricting competition as to price and fixing price in any bidding including cover bidding, bid suppression, bid rotation and market allocation are per se prohibited between competitors without proof of market or outweighing efficiency, while Sec. 4(b) defines agreement to include every tacit, informal, explicit, oral or written concerted action, a rule reinforced for competition policy by Eastern Telecommunications v. ICC (G.R. No. 135992, July 23, 2004) where the Court sustained entry of a qualified rival because no operator is shielded from healthy competition.
Here, the four refiners fixed pump prices and rotated winning bids for municipal fuel in a group chat documented by the finance manager who typed the minutes, which squarely matches price restriction and bid rotation, and the claim that an oral and informal understanding is not an agreement collapses because Sec. 4(b) expressly captures informal, tacit and oral concerted action so no signed pact is required and no weighing of reasonableness is allowed for this track.
The cartel is therefore condemned per se without defining the relevant market or balancing harm against efficiency, and the operative consequence is prohibition of the arrangement with criminal exposure under Sec. 30 of two to seven years plus P50,000,000 to P250,000,000 for knowing participants.

stem: Two cement makers divide towns by buyer with one taking north distributors and the other taking south distributors. A new entrant proves the division, and the makers answer that no price was ever fixed. Must the Commission still weigh effects before condemning the pact.
answer:
Yes. The Commission must still define the relevant market and weigh effects before condemning the pact, and the absence of any price fixing does not save the buyer-division because market sharing is tested under a different paragraph.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 14(b)(2), approved July 21, 2015, dividing or sharing the market by volume, territory, type of goods, buyers, sellers or any other means between competitors is prohibited only where it has the object or effect of substantially preventing, restricting or lessening competition, while Sec. 26 requires the Commission to define the relevant market and determine substantial adverse impact outweighing efficiency gains with a forward-looking totality review, a pro-rivalry approach confirmed in Eastern Telecommunications v. ICC (G.R. No. 135992, July 23, 2004) where the Court rejected any vested right to a fenced service area.
Here, the two cement makers divided towns by buyer with one taking north distributors and the other taking south distributors as proved by the new entrant, which fits market division by buyers and territory, and the counter-reading that no price was ever fixed misses the track because price fixing belongs to Sec. 14(a) per se while this buyer allocation lives under Sec. 14(b) where substantial lessening through object or effect is still required.
The pact is therefore condemned only after the Sec. 26 weighing finds substantial harm outweighing any proven efficiency, and the operative consequence is a Commission prohibition order against the division with the makers barred from enforcing the allocation.

stem: A dominant flour mill sells below cost for six months with internal memos targeting the death of a new rival mill. A second dominant mill only matches the first mill price in good faith for comparable flour. Which mill abuses its position.
answer:
The first dominant mill abuses while the second dominant mill stays lawful, because destructive object is proved against the predator and good-faith matching shields the responder despite dominance on both sides.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 15(a), approved July 21, 2015, selling goods below cost with the object of driving competition out of the relevant market is prohibited as abuse of dominant position, while the same paragraph expressly saves a price established in good faith to meet or compete with a lower rival price for the same or comparable product of like quality, a conduct-focused test consistent with Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, November 5, 1997) where the Court struck down only entry-entrenching barriers and not size or entry itself.
Here, the first flour mill sold below cost for six months with internal memos targeting the death of the new rival mill, which establishes the prohibited destructive object beyond low price alone, while the second mill only matched the first mill price in good faith for comparable flour, which fits the statutory saving clause, and the counter-reading that dominance alone condemns both fails because dominance without abusive conduct is never punished.
The first mill is therefore liable for abuse with the operative consequence of a Commission cease-and-desist order plus fines and remedies against the predation, while the second mill is cleared because good-faith matching is lawful competition.

stem: A dominant bottler charges provincial dealers a higher price than Manila dealers for identical drinks on identical terms, and the gap tracks no cost, volume, or rival-price difference. The bottler answers that price gaps are normal business. Is the differential permissible.
answer:
No. The differential is not permissible and constitutes abuse of dominant position because it unreasonably discriminates among contemporaneously trading dealers on similar terms with substantial lessening of competition and fits none of the four saving classes.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 15(d), approved July 21, 2015, setting prices that discriminate unreasonably between customers contemporaneously trading on similar terms where the effect may substantially lessen competition is prohibited, with only four permissible differentials for socialized pricing, cost-reflecting differences, responses to rival prices or facilities, and market-driven changes, a strict saving scheme consistent with Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) where the Court required pleaded and proved ultimate facts on market, position and abuse rather than conclusions.
Here, the dominant bottler charged provincial dealers a higher price than Manila dealers for identical drinks on identical terms with the gap tracking no cost, volume, or rival-price difference, which establishes unreasonable discrimination on similar terms, and the counter-reading that price gaps are normal business fails because normalcy is irrelevant unless the gap reasonably reflects cost, answers rivalry, serves socialized pricing, or responds to market conditions.
The differential therefore falls outside every permissible class and is condemned as abuse, with the operative consequence of a Commission order to cease the discrimination, equalize terms or justify a saving differential, plus applicable fines.

stem: Two beverage giants breach both operative thresholds and sign on June 1 with notice filed the same day. They close on June 11 before any decision. The giants claim the ten-day sprint harmed no one. What is the status of the closing.
answer:
The June 11 closing is void and both giants face an administrative fine of one percent to five percent of transaction value, with the thirty-day waiting period violated and the claim of no harm irrelevant to gun-jumping.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 17, approved July 21, 2015, parties breaching the operative thresholds under Sec. 19, currently Size of Party P9,100,000,000 with Size of Transaction P3,800,000,000 effective March 1, 2026, are prohibited from consummating until thirty days after notification with voidness plus one to five percent fine for breach, a waiting protection for rivalry consistent with Eastern Telecommunications v. ICC (G.R. No. 135992, July 23, 2004) where the Court privileged healthy competition over incumbency claims.
Here, the two beverage giants breached both operative thresholds and signed on June 1 with notice filed the same day yet closed on June 11 before any decision, which is only ten days into the thirty-day bar, and the counter-reading that the ten-day sprint harmed no one fails because Sec. 17 punishes the act of early closing itself without requiring proven market harm, leaving merits review still open.
The closing is therefore void ab initio with penalties accruing on transaction value, and the operative consequence is that the parties must unwind or re-notify and wait out the full clock with fines paid while the Commission retains power to prohibit or conditionally clear on merits.

stem: A buyer takes control of a rival in four monthly slices within one year, with each slice below threshold but all four combined above it. The buyer files nothing and claims each slice stands alone. Must the buyer have notified.
answer:
Yes. The buyer was required to notify because the four slices aggregate into one transaction that breached the thresholds, and the claim that each slice stands alone fails against the creeping-transaction rule.
Under PCC IRR Rule 4 Sec. 3(e) implementing R.A. No. 10667 Secs. 17 and 19, approved July 21, 2015, successive transactions or part-acquisitions within one year between the same parties or their controlled entities count as one transaction for notification once the combined value breaches Size of Party P9,100,000,000 with Size of Transaction P3,800,000,000 effective March 1, 2026, an anti-circumvention rule consistent with Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) where the Court looked past bundling form to ultimate market facts.
Here, the buyer took control of a rival in four monthly slices within one year with each slice below threshold but all four combined above it and filed nothing, which triggers aggregation from the step that pushes the total past the thresholds, and the counter-reading that each slice stands alone fails because the rule expressly reckons the one-year window as a single deal to prevent threshold evasion by slicing.
Notification was therefore due before consummating the breaching slice with the operative consequence that the closing without notice is void and draws one to five percent of transaction value, and splitting one takeover into small steps never defeats compulsory notification.
